ipw: Estimate Inverse Probability Weights

ipw

The ipw package provides a flexible toolkit for estimating Inverse Probability Weights (IPW) to fit marginal structural models. Functions to estimate the probability to receive the observed treatment, based on individual characteristics. The inverse of these probabilities can be used as weights when estimating causal effects from observational data via marginal structural models. Both point treatment situations and longitudinal studies can be analysed. The same functions can be used to correct for informative censoring.

Key Features

  • Point Treatment & Longitudinal Data: Functions to handle both static exposures and time-varying confounding.
  • Wide Range of Models: Support for binomial, multinomial, ordinal, and continuous (Gaussian) exposures.
  • Survival Analysis: Integration with Cox proportional hazards models for time-to-event data.
  • Diagnostic Tools: Built-in plotting functions to assess weight stability and the positivity assumption.

Installation 

install.packages("ipw")

Or the development version from GitHub:

# install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("TranHung93/ipw")

Documentation: https://tranhung93.github.io/ipw/; for a walk-through of all features see the vignette, vignette("ipw") or Get started.

Example: Point Treatment Causal Inference

This example simulates data with a continuous confounder (l) and a binomial exposure (a) to estimate a marginal causal effect of 10.

library(ipw)
library(survey)

# 1. Simulate data
set.seed(123)
n <- 1000
simdat <- data.frame(l = rnorm(n, 10, 5))
a.lin <- simdat$l - 10
pa <- exp(a.lin)/(1 + exp(a.lin))
simdat$a <- rbinom(n, 1, prob = pa)
simdat$y <- 10*simdat$a + 0.5*simdat$l + rnorm(n, -10, 5)

# 2. Estimate IPW weights
temp <- ipwpoint(
   exposure = a,
   family = "binomial",
   link = "logit",
   numerator = ~ 1,
   denominator = ~ l,
   data = simdat)

# 3. Fit Marginal Structural Model (MSM)
msm <- svyglm(y ~ a, 
              design = svydesign(~1, weights = ~temp$ipw.weights, data = simdat))

summary(msm)
#> 
#> Call:
#> svyglm(formula = y ~ a, design = svydesign(~1, weights = ~temp$ipw.weights, 
#>     data = simdat))
#> 
#> Survey design:
#> svydesign(~1, weights = ~temp$ipw.weights, data = simdat)
#> 
#> Coefficients:
#>             Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
#> (Intercept)  -6.2885     0.2757  -22.81   <2e-16 ***
#> a            10.6622     0.8083   13.19   <2e-16 ***
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
#> 
#> (Dispersion parameter for gaussian family taken to be 22.76977)
#> 
#> Number of Fisher Scoring iterations: 2

Example: Time-Varying Weights

For longitudinal research, such as the HIV cohort in haartdat, ipwtm calculates the cumulative product of weights over time.

library(ipw)
library(survival)

data(haartdat)

# Estimate time-varying weights for HAART initiation
temp_tm <- ipwtm(
  exposure = haartind,
  family = "survival",
  numerator = ~ sex + age,
  denominator = ~ sex + age + cd4.sqrt,
  id = patient,
  tstart = tstart,
  timevar = fuptime,
  type = "first",
  data = haartdat
)

# Visualize weight stability
ipwplot(weights = temp_tm$ipw.weights, timevar = haartdat$fuptime, 
        binwidth = 100, main = "Stabilized Weights Over Time")

ipw or WeightIt?

WeightIt (Greifer) is a comprehensive R package for weighting, and for many analyses it is the better choice. The two packages overlap for simple cases (a binary point treatment with a logistic model gives the same weights in both) and are complementary otherwise.

Use WeightIt for point treatments when you want machine-learning or balancing methods (generalized boosted models, SuperLearner, BART, CBPS, entropy balancing, energy balancing, and more), a wide choice of estimands, balance diagnostics through cobalt, and outcome models whose standard errors account for the estimation of the weights (glm_weightit(), coxph_weightit(), also for ordinal and multinomial outcomes).

PSweight is another option for point treatments, binary or with several levels: especially for overlap (and matching or entropy) weights with built-in sandwich standard errors that account for the estimated propensity score, augmented (doubly robust) estimators, and survey or clustered data.

Use ipw for

  • exposures that change over time in long (counting-process) data, where each person has their own visit times: ipwtm() fits one model pooled over all rows;
  • Cox models for the time to the first switch of treatment or to censoring (ipwtm(family = "survival"));
  • exposures that switch back and forth or recur (type = "all", including Cox models for recurrent exposure events);
  • count and skewed continuous exposures with built-in models (Poisson, negative binomial, gamma, log-normal);
  • analyses with few dependencies.

A WeightIt analysis of a point treatment, with entropy balancing and an outcome model whose standard errors account for the estimated weights:

W <- WeightIt::weightit(a ~ l, data = simdat, method = "ebal", estimand = "ATE")
fit <- WeightIt::glm_weightit(y ~ a, data = simdat, weightit = W)
summary(fit)$coefficients
#>              Estimate Std. Error   z value      Pr(>|z|)
#> (Intercept) -5.653647  0.3779844 -14.95736  1.394591e-50
#> a           10.684785  0.4998841  21.37453 2.306556e-101

An ipw analysis of time-varying data in long format (one row per patient per interval, as in haartdat above), with weights for starting HAART and for dropout, and a weighted Cox model:

w.start <- ipwtm(exposure = haartind, family = "survival", numerator = ~ sex + age,
                 denominator = ~ sex + age + cd4.sqrt, id = patient,
                 tstart = tstart, timevar = fuptime, type = "first", data = haartdat)
w.drop <- ipwtm(exposure = dropout, family = "survival", numerator = ~ sex + age,
                denominator = ~ sex + age + cd4.sqrt, id = patient,
                tstart = tstart, timevar = fuptime, type = "cens", data = haartdat)
msm.cox <- coxph(Surv(tstart, fuptime, event) ~ haartind + cluster(patient),
                 data = haartdat, weights = w.start$ipw.weights * w.drop$ipw.weights)
summary(msm.cox)$conf.int
#>          exp(coef) exp(-coef) lower .95 upper .95
#> haartind 0.3920629   2.550611 0.1614445 0.9521124
ipw WeightIt
Treatment types binary, multinomial, ordinal, count (Poisson, negative binomial), continuous (normal, gamma, log-normal) binary, multi-category (incl. ordinal), continuous (normal or other conditional density, or kernel density)
Methods parametric models: glm(), multinom(), polr(), glm.nb(), GAMs (mgcv), Cox models; your own probabilities (ipwprobtm()) propensity score models (GLM, GBM, SuperLearner, BART, CBPS, …) and balancing methods (entropy, energy, stable balancing weights, …); user-defined methods
Estimands ATE (stabilized or not); ATT, ATC, ATO for a binary, ATT and ATO for a categorical point treatment ATE, ATT, ATC, ATO, ATM, ATOS (binary); ATE, ATT, ATC, ATO, ATM (multi-category)
Longitudinal data long data, one row per person and interval; individual (irregular) visit times; one model pooled over time (pooled logistic, Cox, multinomial, ordinal, GEE) weightitMSM(): wide data, one row per person, one model per time point (the same time points for everyone); weights multiplied over time points
Censoring censoring weights with the same models, including Cox models (type = "cens") censoring weights with .cens() in weightit() and weightitMSM()
Outcome models and standard errors fit with lm(), glm(), coxph(), svyglm() etc.; ipwvcov() (new) for M-estimation standard errors with a binary point treatment; otherwise the bootstrap glm_weightit(), ordinal_weightit(), multinom_weightit(), coxph_weightit(): M-estimation, robust, bootstrap, fractional weighted bootstrap and cluster-robust standard errors
Trimming truncation at percentiles (trunc) trim() (trimming or truncation)
Diagnostics ipwplot(); balance with cobalt (weights passed as a vector) summary() (weight ranges, effective sample size, …); full cobalt integration
Dependencies MASS, nnet, survival, geepack cobalt, ggplot2, cli, rlang, sandwich, generics, arg, plus optional packages for many methods
License GPL (>= 2) GPL (>= 2)

A side-by-side comparison on the same data, including the standard errors and what longitudinal data with individual visit times mean for each package, is in the article ipw, WeightIt and PSweight side by side, which also shows that PSweight gives the same weights and standard errors as ipw for binary and categorical point treatments.
